2. Brooks Adams was a British official who had served in Bengal.
3. Utsa Patnaik's estimate covers the whole period from the Battle of Plassey (1757) to India's Independence (1947).
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A railway line in colonial India is paid for with money raised from Indian taxpayers, though it mainly serves the colonial power's purposes. How would Utsa Patnaik's estimate of the drain treat this spending?
questions.a: As part of the drain: Indians were charged for it
o: As part of the drain: Indians were charged for it
As a gift from Britain, to be left out of any reckoning of the drain altogether
As money that Britain later paid back to India in full after Independence
As Indian investment in Indians' own welfare, which lies outside the drain

questions.q: A newspaper reports the chapter's figure for Utsa Patnaik's estimate as '45 trillion dollars, in today's value'. Why does the chapter state it in today's value and add that it is about 13 times Britain's GDP in 2023?
questions.a: So that readers can judge the scale of the drain against a present-day economy
o: So that readers can judge the scale of the drain against a present-day economy
Because the dollar was the currency used for trade between India and Britain in 1765
Because Britain's GDP in 2023 was the amount drained from India each year
Because today's value shows how much the Company paid for Indian goods

questions.q:
Match each element of the 1778 painting 'The East offering its riches to Britannia' in Column A with what it symbolises, according to the chapter, in Column B.
Column A: 1. The lion beside Britannia  2. 'Old Father Thames'  3. The god Mercury  4. The low position and bent posture of the colonies
Column B: a. London  b. the colonies' inferior position  c. commerce and travel  d. power

(a) Over which years does the chapter say Utsa Patnaik's estimate of the drain run, and how many years is that? (b) The estimate is 45 trillion U.S. dollars. On average, roughly how much wealth per year does that imply? Round sensibly.
questions.a: (a) 1765 to 1938: 1938 - 1765 = 173 years. (b) 45 / 173 = about 0.26 trillion dollars a year, roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars (in today's value).
s: Part (a): 173 years
Part (b): about 0.26 trillion dollars a year

questions.q:
An imaginary colonial province's yearly accounts (all figures illustrative): taxes collected from Indians, Rs 10 crore. Spending: a war fought by the colonial power, Rs 2.5 crore; railways and a telegraph network laid mainly to serve the colonial power, Rs 3 crore; the colonial administration and its officials, Rs 3.5 crore; village irrigation and schools, Rs 1 crore.
(a) Which two spending lines match the chapter's own examples of what Indians were charged for besides taxes on land?
(b) What percentage of the taxes went on those two lines together?
(c) Explain, using the chapter, why spending on the war counts as part of the drain even though no money was shipped openly to Britain for it.
(d) A student argues: 'The railway money was spent inside India, so it cannot be part of any drain.' Judge her argument.
questions.a: (a) The war, and the railways and telegraph network. (b) (2.5 + 3) / 10 x 100 = 55 per cent. (c) The chapter says wealth was extracted not just through taxes but by charging Indians for the colonial power's expenditures, even on wars; Indians paid for the colonial power's own purposes. (d) Her argument fails: the chapter says Indians were charged for the colonial power's spending on the railways and the telegraph network, which mainly served British interests, so where the money was spent does not settle whom it served.
s: Part (a): the war, and the railways and telegraph
Part (b): 55 per cent
Part (c): charging Indians for the colonial power's expenditures, even wars, is part of the drain
Part (d): fails, since charging Indians for railways serving British interests is part of the drain

questions.q: 'Economic exploitation was not a side effect of British rule in India but its foundation.' Justify this statement using the evidence the chapter gives about the drain of wealth.
questions.a: (1) Brooks Adams wrote that Bengal plunder arrived in London soon after Plassey, and that Britain's industrial revolution began in 1760, funded at least partly by 'stolen wealth from India' (Durant's phrase). (2) William Digby said modern England was made great by Indian wealth taken by the stronger, and that plunder grew worse under the later administrators. (3) Naoroji and Dutt, using British reports, showed many billions of pounds extracted. (4) Patnaik estimates 45 trillion U.S. dollars from 1765 to 1938, about 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP. (5) It was taken not only through taxes but by charging Indians for railways, the telegraph and even wars, so extraction ran through the whole system of rule from Plassey to the 20th century.
s: Adams: plunder after Plassey and the industrial revolution
Digby: England made great by Indian wealth, plunder worse under administrators
Naoroji and Dutt: billions of pounds from British reports
Patnaik's estimate and its scale
Methods built into rule: taxes and charges for railways, telegraph, wars

questions.q: True or False? 'Utsa Patnaik's estimate of the drain is about one-thirteenth of Britain's GDP in 2023.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the estimate, 45 trillion U.S. dollars in today's value for 1765 to 1938, is about 13 times Britain's GDP in 2023, not one-thirteenth of it.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: about 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP

questions.q: The chapter says: 'Had this wealth remained invested in India, it would have been a very different country when it attained Independence.' Give a reason for this view, using one figure from the chapter.
questions.a: The drain moved wealth out of India instead of letting it be invested in India's own development. Patnaik's estimate alone, 45 trillion dollars between 1765 and 1938, is about 13 times Britain's whole GDP in 2023, so its loss left India far poorer than it would otherwise have been.
s: Reason: wealth was moved out instead of invested in India
A figure from the chapter supporting the scale (for example 45 trillion dollars, 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP)

questions.q: The 1778 painting is titled 'The East offering its riches to Britannia'. Write a new title that a historian using this chapter would accept, and justify it with two details from the painting or the chapter.
questions.a: Sample title: 'Britannia Takes the Riches of the East'. Justification: (1) the chapter asks whether the colonies really 'offered' their wealth or whether Britain seized it by force or ruse, and it documents a drain of wealth through plunder and taxes; (2) the painting itself shows Britannia seated higher, with a lion for power, and the colonies lower and bent, which is a picture of domination, not of free giving.
s: A new title that replaces 'offering' with taking or seizing
Justification 1 from the chapter (seized by force or ruse, the drain)
Justification 2 from the painting (height, lion, bent posture)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dadabhai Naoroji's 1901 book compiled estimates of the wealth drained out of India.
Reason (R): The phrase 'stolen wealth from India' was used by the U.S. historian Will Durant.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Kabir writes: 'Brooks Adams believed Britain's industrial revolution was already well under way long before any wealth arrived from Bengal.' Which correction matches what Adams wrote in 1895?
questions.a: Bengal plunder reached London soon after Plassey; revolution began in 1760
o: Bengal plunder reached London soon after Plassey; revolution began in 1760
He said the revolution began in 1760, some thirty years after the Battle of Plassey
He said Indian plunder only sped up a revolution that was already well under way
He said the revolution owed nothing to India and everything to British inventors

questions.q: Sneha says: 'The drain of India's wealth began with the Bengal plunder that reached London soon after Plassey, and it was documented only by Indian writers.' Test each half of her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half fits Brooks Adams, who wrote that very soon after Plassey the Bengal plunder began to arrive in London. The second half is wrong: Adams was a U.S. historian, the phrase 'stolen wealth from India' is by the U.S. historian Will Durant, and William Digby, whom the chapter groups with British officials and public intellectuals, wrote of plunder too. Naoroji took his cue from scholars such as Adams and Digby, R.C. Dutt did a similar exercise, and Utsa Patnaik added a recent estimate.
s: First half right: plunder reached London soon after Plassey (Adams)
Second half wrong: Adams and Durant (U.S.) and Digby (British) also documented it
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: A researcher wants to check where Dadabhai Naoroji found the figures in his book on the drain of India's wealth. Which source does the chapter name?
questions.a: British reports
o: British reports
Records kept by Indian village councils
Ledgers of the French Company in Pondicherry
Letters written by the princely rulers

questions.q: Brooks Adams wrote in 1895 about the profit from the Indian plunder. Which claim does the chapter quote from him?
questions.a: Possibly since the world began no investment had yielded such profit
o: Possibly since the world began no investment had yielded such profit
Indian plunder had yielded only a modest profit that was soon spent
The plunder had yielded less profit than Britain's own factories
The profit had gone mostly to Indian merchants and bankers

questions.q:
A debate team has three unnamed sources on the drain of wealth.
Source P: 'Very soon after Plassey, the Bengal plunder began to arrive in London ... the industrial revolution began with the year 1760.'
Source Q: '... under the later Britons, as administrators ... the plunder is proceeding far more outrageously today than at any preceding period.'
Source R: 'About 45 trillion U.S. dollars (in today's value) was extracted between 1765 and 1938.'
The chapter groups William Digby with the British officials and public intellectuals who denounced the Company's cruelty. Will Durant used 'stolen wealth from India' to say that Britain's industrial revolution was made possible at least partly by that wealth.
(a) Name the writers of Source P and Source Q.
(b) Which source does Durant's phrase sum up?
(c) Which source supports the claim that extraction grew worse once the British became administrators? Quote the words.
(d) The team must answer 'How large was the drain over the colonial period?' with ONE source. Which should they use, and why not the other two?
questions.a: (a) Source P: Brooks Adams, the U.S. historian (1895); Source Q: William Digby (1901). (b) Source P, the only one that links the plunder to the industrial revolution. (c) Source Q: 'proceeding far more outrageously' under 'the later Britons, as administrators'. (d) Source R: it is the only one that gives a total, 45 trillion U.S. dollars over 1765 to 1938; P and Q describe plunder but give no figure for its whole size.
s: Part (a): Adams and Digby
Part (b): Source P, via the industrial revolution link
Part (c): Source Q, with the quoted words
Part (d): Source R, as the only one giving a total over the period

questions.q: (a) The chapter says Britannia is seated higher than the colonies in the painting. What does it say this points to, and what belief does it say the Indian figures' dark complexion reflects? (b) Why does the chapter ask whether the colonies 'really offered' their wealth?
questions.a: (a) It points to Britain's superior power over the colonies; the dark complexion reflects the belief in the superiority of white people over the dark-skinned 'natives'. (b) Because the chapter's evidence, including the drain of wealth by taxes and charges, raises the question whether it was seized by force or ruse and not freely offered.
s: Part (a): superior power, and the belief in white superiority
Part (b): the wealth may have been seized by force or ruse, so 'offering' is questionable

questions.q: Dadabhai Naoroji's book on the drain of wealth appeared in 1901. Brooks Adams had made his remark about the Bengal plunder ___ years earlier.

(a) What link did Brooks Adams draw between the Battle of Plassey and the year 1760? (b) The chapter concludes that Britain's industrial revolution was made possible 'at least partly' by wealth from India. Why is 'at least partly' a careful choice of words?
questions.a: (a) Very soon after Plassey (1757) the Bengal plunder began to arrive in London, and he noted that the industrial revolution began with the year 1760, so he linked the plunder to its start. (b) It claims that Indian wealth was one contribution to a revolution that needed much investment, without claiming it was the only cause; the conclusion stays within what the evidence supports.
s: Part (a): plunder reached London soon after Plassey, and the revolution began in 1760
Part (b): Indian wealth is claimed as one contribution, not the only cause

questions.q: Show that the claim 'India's wealth was drained only through taxes' cannot be supported by the chapter. Give three pieces of evidence.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says the wealth was extracted not just through taxes. (2) Indians were also charged for the colonial power's expenditure on building the railways and the telegraph network. (3) They were charged even for the colonial power's wars.
s: The chapter says not just through taxes
Charges for railways and the telegraph network
Charges for wars

questions.q: Analyse the chapter's account of how India's wealth was drained and what it cost. (a) Name three ways in which wealth was taken. (b) Give the period and the size of Utsa Patnaik's estimate, and the comparison the chapter makes. (c) What does the chapter say would have been different if the wealth had stayed in India? (d) Judge the painting's title 'The East offering its riches to Britannia' in the light of (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Taxes; charging Indians for the colonial power's expenditure on the railways and the telegraph network; charging them even for wars. (b) 1765 to 1938; 45 trillion U.S. dollars in today's value, about 13 times Britain's GDP in 2023. (c) Had the wealth remained invested in India, it would have been a very different country when it attained Independence. (d) The title is misleading: the chapter asks whether the riches were really offered or seized by force or ruse, and the means of extraction and the scale of the drain point to seizure, not a free offering.
s: Part (a): three ways wealth was taken
Part (b): the period 1765 to 1938 and 45 trillion dollars
Part (b): about 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP
Part (c): India would have been a very different country at Independence
Part (d): the title is misleading, since the drain points to seizure

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's textile exports fell sharply in the 19th century.
Reason (R): Indian cotton textiles ranged from ultra-thin muslins to richly embossed fabrics.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Two sources about Indian education around 1830.
Source A: early 19th-century British reports on Indian village schools, where children were taught reading, writing and arithmetic 'upon a system so economical ... and at the same time so simple and effectual'.
Source B: Thomas Macaulay's Minute of 1835: 'a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia'.
(a) How many village schools did the reports count in Bengal and Bihar up to 1830? Give the midpoint of the range.
(b) What did Macaulay admit in the same Minute about his own knowledge, and why does it weaken Source B?
(c) What does the chapter say became of the traditional schools, and what did English become?
(d) A historian wants to know how well ordinary Indian children were being taught in 1830. Which source should she rely on, and why?
questions.a: (a) 100,000 to 150,000; midpoint (100,000 + 150,000) / 2 = 125,000. (b) He admitted he had 'no knowledge of either Sanskrit or Arabic', so he was judging literatures he could not read. (c) India's traditional schools slowly disappeared, and English became a language of prestige associated with the colonial masters. (d) Source A: it reports what was observed in actual village schools, while Source B is an opinion about literature by someone who admitted he could not read it and says nothing about how children were taught.
s: Part (a): 100,000 to 150,000 schools, midpoint 125,000
Part (b): no knowledge of Sanskrit or Arabic, so the judgement is unfounded
Part (c): traditional schools slowly disappeared; English became a language of prestige
Part (d): Source A, as observation of actual schools

questions.q: A student reads that Indian weavers were ruined and asks whether other Indian crafts shared their fate. Which set does the chapter name as meeting similar scenarios?
questions.a: Manufactures of iron, steel, paper and other goods
o: Manufactures of iron, steel, paper and other goods
Manufactures of spices, ivory and sandalwood
Manufactures of rice, wheat and indigo
Manufactures of jute, hemp and coir only

questions.q: A student's chart says: 'India's share of world GDP rose steadily through the colonial period.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: It kept declining under colonial rule, to hardly 5 per cent at Independence
o: It kept declining under colonial rule, to hardly 5 per cent at Independence
It stayed at about one-fourth until Independence and then fell suddenly to 5 per cent
It fell to hardly 5 per cent by the year 1800 and has not changed since then
It fell at first but recovered to about one-fourth again by the time of Independence

questions.q:
Match each feature of pre-colonial India in Column A with what happened to it under colonial rule in Column B.
Column A: 1. Village councils that managed community affairs  2. Customary laws of communities  3. Pathashalas and madrasas  4. Indian textile exports
Column B: a. disregarded by British codes of law  b. replaced by a centralised bureaucracy for tax collection and order  c. slowly disappeared as Macaulay's policy gained the upper hand  d. fell sharply while British imports into India grew

An imaginary weaving town in Bengal had 1,000 working looms in 1800 and only 150 in 1850 (figures illustrative). Its cloth had once been sold in Britain and other parts of the world. By 1850 the market is full of cloth made in British mills.
(a) By what percentage did the number of working looms fall?
(b) Name the two British tariff policies that explain the change.
(c) Besides tariffs, what did Britain control that made it hard for the town's traders to export?
(d) A councillor proposes: 'Let the jobless weavers take up farming on the land around the town.' Judge whether this solves the problem, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) (1,000 - 150) / 1,000 x 100 = 85 per cent. (b) Heavy duties on Indian textiles imported into Britain, and minimal tariffs on British manufactured goods forced on India. (c) Most of the sea trade and the exchange rates. (d) It does not solve the problem: the chapter says artisan communities were forced back to subsistence agriculture on increasingly overtaxed land, so the weavers would be crowding onto land already under heavy tax and would stay poor.
s: Part (a): 85 per cent
Part (b): heavy duties into Britain, minimal tariffs into India
Part (c): sea trade and exchange rates
Part (d): does not solve it, since farming meant overtaxed land and poverty

questions.q:
Read the statements about colonial India's changing landscape.
1. Before the 18th century, India's chief textiles were only cotton and silk.
2. Charles Metcalfe described India's village communities as little republics that collapsed whenever a dynasty fell.
3. India's manufacture of iron, steel and paper suffered a decline similar to that of its textiles.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: (a) India contributed at least one-fourth of world GDP until the 16th century and hardly 5 per cent at Independence. By what factor did its share shrink? (b) The chapter sums up this fall in one sentence about how India's standing among the world's lands changed in less than two centuries. State it.
questions.a: (a) 25 per cent to 5 per cent: 25 / 5 = 5, so the share became about one-fifth of what it was (at least). (b) In less than two centuries, one of the richest lands of the world had become one of the poorest.
s: Part (a): a factor of about 5
Part (b): from one of the richest lands to one of the poorest

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says the railways brought people closer together and integrated India's internal market, and still does not call them a gift to India.' Give the verdict and the evidence.
questions.a: True. The chapter grants that the railways brought people closer together and integrated the internal market, but says they were designed primarily to move raw materials to ports, distribute British goods and move armies, and that most of the cost was paid by Indian tax revenue, so they were not a gift.
s: Verdict: True
Evidence: benefits granted, yet designed for imperial needs and paid for by Indian taxes

questions.q: In 1834 William Bentinck observed: 'The bones of the cotton weavers are bleaching the plains of India.' (a) What was he describing? (b) Why does it matter that he was then Governor-General of India?
questions.a: (a) The ruin and poverty of cotton weavers whose livelihood had collapsed with India's textile industry; the image of bones bleaching the plains describes their plight. (b) The remark came from the head of the colonial government itself, so the ruin cannot be dismissed as exaggeration by critics of British rule.
s: Part (a): weavers dying after losing their livelihood
Part (b): the admission came from the highest colonial official

questions.q: In 1840 a farmer in a village has a dispute over a field boundary. Earlier his village council would have settled it. According to the chapter, what would he now face in a British court?
questions.a: An expensive, slow hearing held in a foreign language
o: An expensive, slow hearing held in a foreign language
A cheaper, quicker hearing, though held in a foreign language
A hearing based on his community's customary law
A free hearing conducted by the village elders

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the British turned India's economy from one kind of system into another. Name both. (b) Explain what the chapter means by India becoming a 'market forced to buy British goods'.
questions.a: (a) From a self-sufficient agricultural system supplemented by craft and manufacture, into a supplier of raw materials for British industry and a market forced to buy British goods. (b) Indians had to buy British manufactured goods, which came in with minimal tariffs, whether or not they preferred them, while their own manufactures were shut out of Britain by heavy duties.
s: Part (a): self-sufficient farming and crafts turned into a raw-material supplier and market
Part (b): a market made to buy British goods, helped by minimal tariffs

questions.q: Explain three ways in which the new colonial education system served British objectives, according to the chapter.
questions.a: (1) It aimed to create a class of Indians who served British interests, 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect'. (2) It produced a pool of Indian clerks and minor officials to staff the lower ranks of the administration at a fraction of the cost of British personnel. (3) It sidelined traditional sources of knowledge and authority, creating generations of Indians disconnected from their own cultural heritage.
s: A class of Indians who would serve British interests
Cheap clerks and minor officials
Traditional knowledge and authority sidelined

questions.q: An imaginary district in 1880 is described: 'Its farmers grow cotton and jute for export. Its people buy cloth made in British mills. A railway runs from its fields straight to the port.' Write a matching description of the same district before colonial rule, with three features that the chapter says such a place would have had.
questions.a: Sample: 'The district fed itself from its own fields, and its weavers made cotton and silk cloth sold across India and abroad. Its village council settled disputes and organised irrigation channels and roads. Goods moved along long-established trade routes to local markets.' Features: a self-sufficient agricultural economy supplemented by crafts; a thriving textile manufacture in demand abroad; village self-governance with public works.
s: Self-sufficient farming supplemented by crafts
Thriving local manufacture, especially textiles
Village councils managing disputes and public works

questions.q: Give a reason why English became 'a language of prestige' under colonial rule, and state the lasting division in Indian society that the chapter links to it.
questions.a: English was associated with the colonial masters, so it carried their power and status as Macaulay's policy spread English education. This created lasting divisions between English-educated elites and the masses.
s: Reason: English was linked to the colonial masters
Division: English-educated elites versus the masses

questions.q: Analyse how colonial rule changed the way Indians were governed and judged. (a) Describe the village councils and the regional administrations that existed before. (b) What replaced them, and for what purpose? (c) How did British codes of law affect ordinary Indians? (d) Why does the chapter call this 'presented as modernisation' and not real improvement?
questions.a: (a) Village councils managed community affairs, resolved disputes and organised public works such as irrigation and roads; regional kingdoms kept complex administrations evolved over centuries for local needs, and Metcalfe called the villages 'little republics'. (b) A centralised bureaucracy designed mainly to facilitate tax collection and maintain order rather than promote public welfare, destroying centuries-old community decision-making. (c) The codes disregarded customary laws, and courts became expensive, time-consuming and conducted in a foreign language, alienating ordinary Indians from justice. (d) A foreign system unsuited to India was imposed under the label of modernising, while it served tax collection and control and left people less able to obtain justice.
s: Part (a): village councils and regional administrations
Part (b): a centralised bureaucracy for tax and order
Part (b): community decision-making destroyed
Part (c): customary law disregarded; costly, slow, foreign-language courts
Part (d): a foreign system imposed in the name of modernisation

questions.q: Show that the claim 'Britain bore the cost of governing India' cannot be supported by the chapter. Give three pieces of evidence.
questions.a: (1) The colonial administrative apparatus was financed by Indian taxation. (2) Military installations and the lavish lifestyles of British officials in India were also paid for by Indian taxes. (3) Most of the railways, and likewise the telegraph, were paid for by Indian tax revenue. The chapter's conclusion: Indians funded their own subjugation.
s: The administration was paid for by Indian taxes
Military installations and officials' lifestyles too
Railways and telegraph paid for by Indian revenue

questions.q: In 1830 an Indian trader in Surat finds that even when he lowers his price for cloth to be shipped to Britain, he cannot export as before. Besides duties, which advantage of Britain does the chapter name as part of the reason?
questions.a: Control of most of the sea trade and of exchange rates
o: Control of most of the sea trade and of exchange rates
Control of all Indian cotton fields
A ban on Indian ships in every Indian port
Ownership of the looms that wove Indian cloth

questions.q: Farhan says: 'The railways were Britain's gift to India. Britain paid for them, and they were laid out to serve the routes Indian traders already used.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. (1) Not a gift: most of the construction was paid for by Indian tax revenue. (2) Not laid out for Indian traders: routes largely ignored existing trade patterns. (3) They were designed primarily to move raw materials from the interior to the ports, spread British goods and move armies, so Indians funded infrastructure that mainly served British interests.
s: Paid for mostly by Indian tax revenue
Routes ignored existing trade patterns
Designed for British purposes; verdict No

questions.q: 'In less than two centuries, one of the richest lands of the world had become one of the poorest.' Justify this statement from the chapter, using industry, trade policy and the colonial economy.
questions.a: (1) Before the 18th century India was renowned for manufacturing, especially textiles of cotton, silk, wool, jute, hemp and coir, from ultra-thin muslins to embossed fabrics, in demand worldwide. (2) Britain imposed heavy duties on Indian textiles entering Britain and forced India to take British goods at minimal tariffs, and controlled sea trade and exchange rates. (3) Textile exports fell sharply while British imports rose even more sharply; artisans were pushed into subsistence farming on overtaxed land, and iron, steel and paper declined too. (4) The economy was rebuilt as a supplier of raw materials and a captive market, with railways and administration paid for by Indian taxes. (5) India's share of world GDP fell from at least one-fourth to hardly 5 per cent at Independence.
s: India's earlier manufacturing strength
British duties, tariffs and control of trade and exchange rates
Collapse of exports and ruin of artisans, with other industries
Economy reshaped as raw-material supplier and market, paid for by Indians
GDP share from one-fourth to about 5 per cent

questions.q: A colonial engineer in 1855 explains a new railway line: 'It lets us rush soldiers from their cantonments to a far-off uprising.' Which stated purpose of the railways does this show?
questions.a: Moving armies quickly to fight a distant rebellion or war
o: Moving armies quickly to fight a distant rebellion or war
Integrating the Indian market for the benefit of Indian traders
Following the trade routes Indian merchants had always used
Carrying Indian-made manufactures to Britain's ports

questions.q: (a) Give two reasons why Charles Metcalfe called India's village communities 'little republics'. (b) Using (a), explain what was lost when the British replaced them with a centralised bureaucracy.
questions.a: (a) They had nearly everything they wanted within themselves, and they lasted where nothing else lasted: dynasties and revolutions came and went, but the village community remained, and Metcalfe credited them with the preservation of the people of India. (b) Self-reliant community decision-making (councils that settled disputes and organised irrigation and roads) was replaced by a bureaucracy built mainly for tax collection and order rather than public welfare, destroying centuries-old mechanisms that had kept communities going.
s: Part (a): self-sufficient and long-lasting through changes of rulers
Part (b): community self-government and public works replaced by a tax-and-order bureaucracy

questions.q: A forest officer in the 1840s forbids a tribal village from gathering forest produce and demands its taxes in cash. Which two threats from the chapter's account of British policy towards tribal communities does this show?
questions.a: Restricted access to forests and forest produce, and cash taxes
o: Restricted access to forests and forest produce, and cash taxes
Replacement of tribal councils, and conversion by missionaries
Labelling as 'criminal tribes', and debt traps
Turning tribal land into private property, and forced indigo growing

questions.q:
Match each movement in Column A with the grievance that set it off in Column B.
Column A: 1. Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion  2. Kol Uprising  3. Santhal Rebellion  4. Indigo Revolt
Column B: a. moneylenders and landlords taking ancestral lands with British support  b. peasants forced to abandon food crops for a dye crop  c. new land and tax policies restricting free movement for pilgrimage and charity  d. land policies that favoured outsiders over the original inhabitants

(a) What did a colonial law do to hundreds of tribal communities, and with what result? (b) Besides that law, the British described tribals as 'primitive'. What do these two British actions have in common?
questions.a: (a) It categorised them as 'criminal tribes', so they were unjustly harassed for decades. (b) Both described whole communities in a negative way, and both were followed by harsh treatment of them: harassment under the law, and efforts to 'civilise' and convert them.
s: Part (a): labelled 'criminal tribes', harassed for decades
Part (b): both labels branded whole communities and justified control over them

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says the Santhal Rebellion was crushed with great violence, yet it still inspired other tribal communities.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. After initial losses the British burned entire villages and killed thousands of Santhals, including the rebel leaders, but the chapter says the daring rebellion inspired other tribal communities to resist colonial rule.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the rising was crushed, but it inspired other tribal communities

questions.q: Which of these was NOT part of the British response to the Santhal Rebellion, as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: A treaty restoring Santhal ancestral lands
o: A treaty restoring Santhal ancestral lands
Burning entire Santhal villages after initial losses
Killing thousands of Santhals
Eventually killing the rebel leaders, Sidhu and Kanhu

questions.q:
An imaginary indigo peasant in northern Bengal in the 1850s (figures illustrative). The planter forces him to grow indigo on his best field instead of rice. Each year the planter pays him Rs 20 for the crop, but growing it costs him Rs 25 in seed, labour and bullocks. He started with a debt of Rs 30 to the planter, and each year's shortfall is added to it.
(a) How much does he lose each year on the indigo crop?
(b) What is his debt after 4 years, if no interest is charged?
(c) Using (a) and (b) and the chapter, explain what the chapter means by 'debt slavery'.
(d) The planter tells him: 'Keep growing indigo and your debt will be cleared in time.' Judge this claim using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) 25 - 20 = Rs 5 a year. (b) 30 + 4 x 5 = Rs 50. (c) Each year he falls deeper into debt to the planter and cannot repay, so he is bound to keep growing indigo: the chapter says everyone from planters to traders profited except the peasants, who were so poorly paid that they were trapped in debt slavery. (d) The claim is false: the crop loses him Rs 5 a year, so his debt rises from Rs 30 to Rs 50 in four years instead of falling.
s: Part (a): Rs 5 a year
Part (b): Rs 50
Part (c): poorly paid peasants trapped in ever-growing debt
Part (d): false, since the debt rises every year

questions.q: A student says: 'The Mundas and Oraons took no part in any rising against the British before 1857.' Which fact from the chapter contradicts this?
questions.a: They are named among the Kol tribes of the Kol Uprising of 1831 to 1832
o: They are named among the Kol tribes of the Kol Uprising of 1831 to 1832
They were among the tribes led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu in the Santhal Rebellion
They were the peasants forced to give up food crops and grow indigo in northern Bengal
They were the ascetics whose free movement was restricted after the famine of 1770

questions.q: The Kol Uprising began in 1831 in Chota Nagpur; the Santhal Rebellion began ___ years later.

Two descriptions of the same movement in Bengal in the late 18th century.
Description 1 (an imaginary British report): 'Bands of bandits dressed as holy men are raiding our treasuries and robbing our collectors.'
Description 2 (an imaginary village storyteller): 'Our holy men were stopped from walking to the shrines and giving alms as they always had. Then they took up arms against the treasuries.'
(a) Who were the sannyasis and fakirs, and what did they traditionally travel for?
(b) What, according to the chapter, restricted their movements?
(c) Why should a historian not simply accept the word 'bandits' in Description 1?
(d) A textbook writer must choose one word for the movement: 'banditry' or 'rebellion'. Which does the chapter use, and why does Description 2 support the choice?
questions.a: (a) Sannyasis were Hindu ascetics and fakirs Muslim ascetics; they traditionally travelled freely for pilgrimage and charity. (b) The East India Company's policies, especially its new land and taxation policies. (c) 'Bandits' is what the British, the side attacked, called them; it hides the grievance and the targets, and the chapter notes that the rebels' precise motivations have been debated. (d) Rebellion: the chapter calls it one of the earliest organised resistance movements, the Sannyasi (or Sannyasi-Fakir) Rebellion; Description 2 shows a grievance, restricted travel for pilgrimage and charity, behind the attacks, which fits a rebellion against policy and not plain banditry.
s: Part (a): Hindu and Muslim ascetics travelling for pilgrimage and charity
Part (b): new Company land and tax policies
Part (c): 'bandits' is the attackers' label that hides the grievance and targets
Part (d): rebellion, supported by the grievance in Description 2

questions.q:
Read the statements about early resistance to British rule.
1. The Kol Uprising broke out in Bengal soon after the famine of 1770.
2. The Mundas and Oraons were among the Kol tribes.
3. The indigo peasants' cause was supported by educated Bengalis and the Bengali press.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: 'Almost from the beginning of British rule, people whose rights or means of living were threatened rose against it.' Justify this statement using all four movements in the chapter's section on early resistance (the Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion, the Kol Uprising, the Santhal Rebellion and the Indigo Revolt).
questions.a: (1) Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion: from after the 1770 famine in Bengal, ascetics whose free travel for pilgrimage and charity was restricted by new land and tax policies attacked treasuries and tax collectors for three decades. (2) Kol Uprising, 1831 to 1832, Chota Nagpur: land policies favoured outsiders over the original tribal inhabitants. (3) Santhal Rebellion, 1855 to 1856: moneylenders and landlords, backed by the British, took Santhal ancestral lands. (4) Indigo Revolt, 1859 to 1862: European planters forced Bengal peasants to grow indigo instead of food and trapped them in debt. In each case a right or means of living (free movement, land, food crops) was threatened, and the risings began soon after the Company took over Bengal's revenue and recurred for nearly a century (1770s to 1862).
s: Sannyasi-Fakir: movement restricted by land and tax policies
Kol: land policies favouring outsiders
Santhal: ancestral lands taken by moneylenders and landlords
Indigo: forced cultivation and debt
Conclusion: lost livelihoods and an early, recurring pattern

questions.q: (a) Put the four movements in order of when they began: Santhal Rebellion, Indigo Revolt, Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion, Kol Uprising. (b) Which two began within four years of each other?
questions.a: (a) Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion (after the famine of 1770), Kol Uprising (1831), Santhal Rebellion (1855), Indigo Revolt (1859). (b) The Santhal Rebellion and the Indigo Revolt: 1859 - 1855 = 4 years.
s: Part (a): the correct order
Part (b): Santhal and Indigo, 4 years apart

questions.q: (a) What, according to the chapter, replaced traditional tribal councils under British rule? (b) Using (a), explain why this threatened the tribes' way of life.
questions.a: (a) The British legal system. (b) The councils had decided community matters in the tribes' own way; replacing them with a foreign legal system took decisions out of the community's hands and went with other pressures the chapter lists, such as loss of forest access and land, so it threatened the tribes' traditional way of life.
s: Part (a): the British legal system
Part (b): community decision-making replaced by a foreign system, adding to other pressures

questions.q: An 1856 sketch in a London magazine, drawn from the artist's imagination, shows Santhal rebels facing gun-wielding sepoys. Which question should a historian ask first about this picture?
questions.a: What image of the Santhals would it create among British readers?
o: What image of the Santhals would it create among British readers?
How many Santhals and how many sepoys fought in the battle it shows?
On which exact day and at which place was the battle fought?
Which Santhal leader posed for the artist?

questions.q: Neel says: 'The indigo peasants won some relief, educated Bengalis backed them, and the Santhals' rising ended in a negotiated settlement.' Test each part of his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first two parts are right: the British authorities were eventually forced to restrict some of the worst abuses, and the peasants' cause was supported by educated Bengalis and the Bengali press. The third is wrong: after initial losses the British burned entire Santhal villages and killed thousands, including the leaders, so the rising was crushed, not settled by agreement.
s: Relief: some of the worst abuses restricted
Educated Bengalis and the Bengali press backed the peasants
Santhals were crushed, not settled; verdict partly right

questions.q: Show that the claim 'British rule met no organised resistance until 1857' cannot be supported by the chapter. Give three pieces of evidence.
questions.a: (1) The Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion began in Bengal after the famine of 1770 and lasted over three decades. (2) The Kol Uprising of 1831 to 1832 in Chota Nagpur saw the Kol tribes control significant territory for a time. (3) The Santhal Rebellion of 1855 to 1856 saw the Santhals declare their own government. The chapter says resistance began almost from the beginning of the British conquest.
s: Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion from after 1770 for three decades
Kol Uprising of 1831 to 1832
Santhal Rebellion of 1855 to 1856

questions.q: Compare the Kol Uprising and the Santhal Rebellion, and analyse what their story shows about British rule. Cover (a) when and where each took place, (b) the cause and leadership of each, (c) how each ended, and (d) what the Santhal Rebellion left behind.
questions.a: (a) Kol: 1831 to 1832 in Chota Nagpur, in present-day Jharkhand. Santhal: 1855 to 1856, across parts of present-day Jharkhand, Bihar and West Bengal. (b) Kol: land policies that favoured outsiders; the Kol tribes included the Mundas and Oraons. Santhal: moneylenders and landlords taking ancestral lands with British support, led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, who declared their own government. (c) The Kols temporarily controlled significant territory before British forces defeated them; the British, after initial losses, burned Santhal villages and killed thousands, including the leaders. (d) It inspired other tribal communities to resist. Together they show British policy taking tribal land and answering resistance with overwhelming force.
s: Part (a): dates and places of both
Part (b): causes of both
Part (b): Santhal leadership and own government
Part (c): how each was defeated
Part (d): inspiration to other tribes, and what this shows about British rule

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion later inspired Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel Anandamath.
Reason (R): The song 'Vande Mataram' became India's national song after Independence.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Why did the British nickname India 'the jewel in the crown of the British Empire'? (b) The chapter describes the British as a 'self-imposed guest'. What point does that phrase make?
questions.a: (a) India was an enormous source of wealth and of natural and human resources for them. (b) A guest is someone invited; the British had invited themselves and stayed as rulers, so the resistance movements were trying to repel an unwanted intruder.
s: Part (a): an enormous source of wealth and resources
Part (b): the British were uninvited rulers, not real guests

questions.q: Write an imaginary diary entry (four or five lines) by a peasant in northern Bengal in 1859 that shows three causes of the Indigo Revolt as the chapter gives them.
questions.a: Sample: 'The planter's men came again today. They say I must plant indigo on my rice field, or my hut will burn. Last year they paid so little for the leaves that I had to borrow, and now I owe more than I can ever repay. My neighbour who refused is in the planter's lock-up. How will my children eat?' Causes shown: forced to abandon food crops for indigo; so poorly paid that he is trapped in debt; refusal punished by imprisonment and destruction of property.
s: Forced to grow indigo instead of food crops
Poor payment leading to debt slavery
Refusal punished by imprisonment, torture or destruction of property

questions.q: The Vellore Mutiny came in 1806; the Great Rebellion broke out ___ years later.
In a class discussion, Aditya argues that India's stolen artefacts have been better preserved in European museums than they would have been at home. How does the chapter itself treat this question?
questions.a: It calls the removal theft and a loss, but leaves repatriation open
o: It calls the removal theft and a loss, but leaves repatriation open
It agrees that the artefacts are better kept where they are now in Europe
It demands that every artefact be returned to India at once
It says that colonial powers took no artefacts from India at any time

questions.q: A museum caption reads: 'The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857: a revolt of soldiers against their officers.' Which fact from the chapter best shows that this caption is too narrow?
questions.a: Rulers such as Rani Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal resisted too
o: Rulers such as Rani Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal resisted too
The officers of the Company's army were almost all British, not Indian
Mangal Pandey attacked British officers at Barrackpore
Sepoys at Meerut killed their own British officers and marched to Delhi

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The British response to the Great Rebellion caused vastly more deaths than the rebels had inflicted.
Reason (R): The British limited their response to recapturing Delhi in September 1857.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: An imaginary Indian newspaper of late 1858 carries the headline: 'Queen's promises cannot be trusted, warns Begum'. Write the three-sentence report that should follow, using facts from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: 'In November, Queen Victoria proclaimed the end of the East India Company's rule in India, promising not to interfere in religious matters and to include more Indians in the administration. Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh, whose kingdom the British annexed and who led the defence of Lucknow, has answered with a counter-proclamation. She warns Indians not to trust such assurances, as "it is the unvarying custom of the English never to forgive a fault be it great or small".'
s: Victoria's proclamation and its two promises
Who the Begum is (Awadh annexed, defence of Lucknow)
Her warning, in her words or close to them

questions.q: (a) What reason do some historians give for the failure of the Great Rebellion? (b) The sepoys at Delhi proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader, but military decisions were taken by the commanders. Explain how this fact supports the reason in (a).
questions.a: (a) The sepoys lacked a unified command and a consistent strategy, despite some heroic leaders. (b) The proclaimed leader was elderly and politically powerless and did not direct the fighting, while separate commanders decided military matters, so there was no single authority to coordinate the rising across many cities.
s: Part (a): no unified command or consistent strategy
Part (b): a powerless figurehead and separate commanders meant no single coordinating authority

questions.q:
A school history club is making posters on the leaders of 1857. The British army officer who commanded the attack on Jhansi wrote that Rani Lakshmibai was 'most dangerous of all the rebel leaders ... best and bravest of the rebels'. One poster draft reads: 'The last rebel leader to keep fighting in the field was Rani Lakshmibai.'
(a) What was Rani Lakshmibai fighting to prevent, and what did she achieve at Gwalior?
(b) Who assisted her, and how long did he go on fighting?
(c) The Crown's proclamation ending Company rule came in November 1858. How many months before it did she die?
(d) Judge the poster draft, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The British annexation of her kingdom of Jhansi; she escaped besieged Jhansi and conquered the Gwalior fort, seizing its treasury and arsenal. (b) Tatia (Tantia) Tope, Nana Saheb's military adviser; he continued fighting until early 1859, was betrayed and handed over to the British, who hanged him. (c) She was killed on 18 June 1858; June to November is 5 months. (d) The draft is wrong: she died in June 1858, while Tatia Tope kept fighting until early 1859, so he, not she, was the last of these two to hold out in the field.
s: Part (a): annexation of Jhansi; Gwalior fort, treasury and arsenal
Part (b): Tatia Tope, fighting until early 1859
Part (c): 5 months
Part (d): wrong, since Tatia Tope outlasted her

questions.q: Which of these was NOT a result of the events of 1858, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Company was given full control of the reorganised Indian Army
o: The Company was given full control of the reorganised Indian Army
The British Crown took direct control of India from the Company
British policy shifted from expansion to consolidating control
The Indian Army was reorganised to prevent unified resistance in future

questions.q: In 1857 a sepoy at Barrackpore, angered by rumours about greased cartridges, attacks his British officers. What does the chapter say followed for him, and with what effect on the other sepoys?
questions.a: He was executed, and the execution spread discontent among the sepoys
o: He was executed, and the execution spread discontent among the sepoys
He was pardoned, and the pardon calmed the discontent among all the other sepoys
He escaped to Delhi, where the sepoys proclaimed him their leader at once
He was dismissed from service, and the other sepoys welcomed the decision

questions.q: True or False? 'Since the rebellion of 1857 failed, the chapter treats it as having no lasting importance.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter calls it a turning point: it sowed a seed for the idea that foreign domination was unacceptable, which grew early in the 20th century into a full-fledged struggle for freedom, and in 1858 it led the Crown to take direct control from the Company.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a turning point that sowed the idea that foreign rule was unacceptable (and ended Company rule)

questions.q:
Read the statements about the outbreak of the Great Rebellion.
1. At Meerut, some sepoys killed their British officers and marched to nearby Delhi.

questions.q: Describe three actions of the British response to the Great Rebellion, as the chapter gives them.
questions.a: (1) The recapture of Delhi in September 1857, with house-to-house massacres. (2) Mass executions at Kanpur, designed to strike terror in the population. (3) A long punitive campaign in which villages were burned and crops destroyed, causing countless deaths, vastly more than those inflicted by the rebels.

Mass executions at Kanpur to strike terror

questions.q: (a) Name two things about India that the British systematically documented, according to the chapter. (b) Identify the flaw the chapter finds in one of these records, and explain it.
questions.a: (a) Any two: the geography of the Subcontinent (meticulous surveys); lists of all ethnic groups; India's monuments, their art and architecture. (b) The lists of ethnic groups were flawed because they rested on unscientific but then prevalent notions of 'race'; genetics has shown that 'races' do not exist.
s: Part (a): two things documented
Part (b): ethnic lists flawed by the unscientific idea of 'race'

questions.q: Tara says: 'The chapter accepts that colonial rule had some beneficial effects, but unintended ones, not part of its aims.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, the claim holds. The chapter calls colonial rule a process of subjugation and exploitation, not a 'civilising mission'. It then lists 'largely unintended consequences': India was opened (or re-opened) to the world and the world to India; the British surveyed the land, documented monuments, restored some ruined ones and initiated archaeology; and translations of Sanskrit texts spread Indian thought in Europe. These benefits came as side effects, not as aims.
s: Colonial rule described as subjugation and exploitation, not a civilising mission
Benefits named: opening to the world, surveys, archaeology, Sanskrit translations
The chapter calls them largely unintended; verdict yes

questions.q: Differentiate between the killings at Kanpur by the rebels and the British mass executions at Kanpur, as the chapter describes them.
questions.a: The rebels under Nana Saheb first agreed to give British civilians safe passage, then massacred over 200 men, women and children, for reasons that are still debated. The British, after regaining control, conducted mass executions at Kanpur designed to strike terror into the population, as part of a punitive campaign whose deaths vastly exceeded those inflicted by the rebels.
s: Rebels: over 200 civilians killed after a promise of safe passage, reasons debated
British: mass executions meant to terrorise the population, part of a far deadlier campaign

questions.q: 'The Great Rebellion of 1857 failed, yet it was a turning point.' Justify this statement. Cover its causes, its spread, its suppression, the reason it failed, and what changed afterwards.
questions.a: Causes: long discontent (Vellore, 1806), farming families hurt by land revenue policy, resentment at annexations, and in 1857 the rumour of cartridges greased with cow and pig fat; Mangal Pandey's attack and execution. Spread: Meerut sepoys killed their officers, marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar; the revolt took Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi, with leaders like Rani Lakshmibai, Tatia Tope and Begum Hazrat Mahal. Suppression: Delhi retaken in September 1857 with house-to-house massacres, mass executions at Kanpur, villages burned and crops destroyed. Failure: some historians say the sepoys lacked a unified command and consistent strategy. Turning point: it sowed the idea that foreign domination was unacceptable, which grew into the 20th-century freedom struggle; in 1858 the Crown took direct control, policy shifted to consolidation and the army was reorganised.
s: Causes, long-term and immediate
Spread and leaders
Brutal suppression
Reason for failure
Turning point: the idea of resisting foreign rule and the changes of 1858

questions.q:
In November 1858 Queen Victoria issued a proclamation ending the East India Company's rule in India. She promised non-interference in religious matters and greater inclusion of Indians in the administration. The British also reorganised the Indian Army in these years. A British official argues: 'The Queen's promise on religion will keep the sepoys loyal, so the army needs no change.'
(a) What period of Indian history did the Crown's takeover begin, and what change of direction in British policy did the chapter note?
(b) Give two sources of sepoy discontent from the chapter, one religious and one economic.
(c) Which of the two does the Queen's promise on religion address?
(d) Judge the official's argument, and say what the chapter says the British did to the army, and why.
questions.a: (a) The British Raj; British policies shifted from aggressive territorial expansion to the consolidation of control. (b) Religious: the 1806 uniform regulations at Vellore, or the 1857 rumour about cartridges greased with cow and pig fat. Economic: most sepoys came from agricultural families suffering hardship under British land revenue policy. (c) Only the religious one. (d) The argument is weak: the promise leaves the economic grievance untouched, and the chapter says the British themselves reorganised the Indian Army so as to prevent unified resistance in the future, so they did not rely on promises alone.
s: Part (a): the Raj; from expansion to consolidation
Part (b): one religious and one economic cause
Part (c): the religious cause only
Part (d): weak, since the economic grievance remains and the army was reorganised to prevent unified resistance

questions.q: Weigh the legacy of European colonialism in India as the chapter does. (a) State the chapter's main verdict and its reason for rejecting the 'civilising mission'. (b) Describe two largely unintended consequences. (c) Explain why the taking of artefacts is presented as double-edged. (d) Does the chapter treat the unintended consequences as balancing the verdict of subjugation? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Colonial rule was a process of subjugation and exploitation executed systematically, with brutal repression if necessary; it was not a 'civilising mission', since India's own civilisation was much older than Europe's. Except for a small elite, Indians suffered abuse, exploitation, violence and uprooting. (b) Any two: India opened (or re-opened) to the world; meticulous surveys; documentation and restoration of monuments and the start of archaeology; the spread of Sanskrit texts to Europe. (c) Thousands of statues, paintings, jewels and manuscripts were stolen, a profound cultural loss and violation of heritage, yet this also promoted some appreciation of Indian art in Europe; repatriation is still debated. (d) No. The chapter calls colonial rule subjugation and exploitation executed systematically, not a 'civilising mission'; it calls the good effects 'largely unintended', and the theft of thousands of artefacts accompanied them, a profound cultural loss.
s: Part (a): subjugation and exploitation; India's older civilisation
Part (b): two unintended consequences
Part (c): theft and loss
Part (c): yet appreciation of Indian art abroad
Part (d): no, with two reasons (systematic subjugation; effects unintended and alongside theft)

questions.q: (a) Which kingdom did Begum Hazrat Mahal belong to, and what had the British done to it? (b) What does her counter-proclamation of 1858 suggest about how she regarded the Queen's promises?
questions.a: (a) Awadh, in the north-central part of present-day Uttar Pradesh; the British had annexed it. (b) She distrusted them: she warned Indians not to trust such assurances, as 'it is the unvarying custom of the English never to forgive a fault be it great or small'.
s: Part (a): Awadh, annexed by the British
Part (b): she warned Indians not to trust the assurances

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'The rebellion of 1857 came out of nowhere. A single rumour about rifle cartridges set it off, and there had been no discontent among the sepoys before.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. (1) There were earlier signs of severe discontent, beginning with the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 over uniform rules that violated Hindu and Muslim religious practice. (2) Most sepoys came from agricultural families suffering great hardship from British land revenue policy, so 1857 followed decades of increasing frustration. (3) The cartridge rumour was the trigger, not the cause; resentment at annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse also contributed to the rebellion.
s: Earlier discontent: the Vellore Mutiny of 1806
Long-term hardship of sepoys' farming families from land revenue policy
The rumour was a trigger after decades of frustration; verdict No
